blocks.x: We're on. You're on? Okay. Let's see. We're recording today in room 104 of the History Building, Tulane University. What's the date anyway? I forgot. November? 25th. The 25th, huh? And let me see now. It's 1959. I said, what else do we want to put down? I forgot that for a minute. We're about to get everybody's name down. Moose, what's your name?
Emmanuel Joseph Zainco.
Everybody calls you Moose.
Moose, I see.
How many people know your real name in the music business? Very few?
Very, very few, yeah.
You like it that way?
I like it that way.
Okay. And Paul? Paul Crawford. And I'm Dick Conner. Moose, when were you born?
I was born February the 12th, 1929.
And where were you born?
Out in Metro, Louisiana. I lived in Metro about, oh, I'd say 22 years or so. And after I'd gotten out of the service, I moved into the city of New Orleans. And I've been living there ever since.
And let's see now. What's your present address, Moose?
4659 Eastern Street. That's in the Gentilly section.
And where were you, when did you first hear any music? When?

Well, that's going to be kind of hard to say, because being in New Orleans, I mean, you're just naturally brought up around music, see. I guess the parades, that's probably the first real spirited music I ever heard, and I took a liking to, you know.
Your mother and father didn't play and hang around the house, or uncles or aunts, anybody
like that? No, as far as I know, I'm about the only one that ever invested $60 in a horn, you know. I'm about the only one that plays anything.
Do you remember any of the parade bands you heard?
Offhand, no. I mean, most of them, I think, might have been high school bands, you know, high school bands from the city.
Not the colored parades? No, no, unfortunately. They don't have a lot of metry very much, I guess, at that, no.

Once in a while you might run up on a good old time guitar player, or maybe fellas that had played years before, you know, they aren't active now, of course, but you might just run up on one every once in a while, you know, and you hear some real good musicians.
Well, how'd you get started on trumpet?

Well, quite a few years ago, I just happened to be downtown, and I saw this fine looking trumpet in the show window. And, of course, I didn't know anything about music, couldn't play, but I just fell in love with the looks of the horn, see. So, I went and invested a few dollars, and I just had to learn to play it, see. I mean, I couldn't see letting that money just lay around doing nothing, so I did learn to play the horn.
Did you study from anybody?
No, no, I play strictly by, yeah. Everything I play is by, yeah.
Well, did anybody help you at all on putting the horn in the right position on your lips? No. Fingering?
Well, I tell you, after playing it about seventeen years, I still don't know if I've got the right position.
Seventeen years ago, it started about, huh? Who did you hear that influenced you on trumpet at first?

Well, I can't think of any one in particular, but I always did like the way Bung Johnson played, and of course I also liked the Baidebeck style. So what I try to do is combine the two together, and sometimes I'll come up with something maybe worthwhile listening to. Bung Baidebeck.
Bung Baidebeck.
Bung Baidebeck. That's what they call you. That's my alias. Let's see now.
When did you start playing, even amateur groups, not professional?

Well, I think the first actual band that I ever played with was about nineteen, nineteen forty-nine. We had a four-piece group out in Metry. And well over a period of years, some of the boys got married, some went in the service, and we just dispersed. And I've been lucky enough to run up on another group that I play with now. So I guess that's about the extent of my band work, 1949 and 1959.
Did you stay with that first group until you got with that bunch before you got into Straws?
No, we just played together, I'd say about maybe a year, two years, you know.
As far as you play in the meantime.

Well, I just put the horn in the case. I hadn't touched it in quite a few years. Well, since I've been playing with the Straws, it's the first time I really got back to playing again. Well, of course we fooled around at the firehouse now. But, I mean, maybe once a week, maybe once a month, you know, it wasn't anything steady. It was just for kicks, you know, we'd sit around and play.
Before you go on, I think we ought to put down Moose's job, what he does for the life. Yeah. Tell him what you want.
Well, I'm a fireman on the New Orleans Fire Department. I've been on that job now six years.
What station you went at?
I'm at Central Fire Station right on Decatur Street in the heart of the French Quarter. Pass that large ass trail, Pa.
Uh-uh.

Thank you. Well, since this is gonna be something concerning Austria, maybe I should say Docker. Dunker. Anyway, uh, what do you do in the fire department there?
