cleaning quarters up. Occasionally you do make a fire, you know.
But you have some time on your hands.
Oh yeah, I have quite a lot of time.
Well, who plays down there, the banjo playing piano players?

Well, they had this captain by the name of Martin Finity. He used to be a banjo player years ago. And when I decided to bring my horn around the firehouse one day, he said he would bring his banjo. So between the two of us, we'd worked up a duet. So in the meantime, this other fella, he's a lieutenant by the name of Del Paget, Sidney Del Paget. He's the drummer. He can't buy what he said. Incidentally, Del Paget used to play with this Evolution Trio that was the craze of New Orleans many years ago. He played with the Evolution Trio. Of course, that was before my time, but they tell me they were great.
I don't think I met him. He wasn't there the night I was down there.

I don't believe it, no. That's probably the first drummer you've ever seen with two fingers off his right hand. But he was terrific. And, oh, occasionally other fellas would drop in, you know, and we'd get a little session going. You know, just by our own amusement. I mean, a firehouse can get to be a pretty dead place, you know. And we'd get a little session going just by our own kicks.
Do you know any more about the Evolution Trio?

No, I'm sorry to say. At one time, I think they might have been the staff orchestra of WWL. That's many years ago. And they did somewhat of a minstrel routine with their playing. And people I have talked to over the years, I mean, they seem to think that these guys were the thing at that time. I couldn't give you dates. I don't know dates. I don't know places that they played. But, uh...
What's the lieutenant's name? Do you know his floor name?
Uh, Sidney Delpaget.
Yeah, you said that. I just missed it.

Yeah, I... Then, uh... They used clarinet, drum, and, uh... Banjo. Now, the banjo player lives someplace up in Kenner right now, I believe. I don't know if he plays anymore, but, uh... He lives up in Kenner somewhere.
We found him. Didn't you tell me once you played in Kenner some? With the band?

Well, that was a part of this little group we had out in Metro. Some of the bars were from Kenner, you know, and, uh... After, well, a couple years, you know, you get to meet one of the fellas. Well, let's start playing again, you know. And you might go sit in somebody's house and play a little bit, you know. But, I mean, as far as steady work, we've never ever done anything steady. Just for our own amusement. That's about... That was about the extent of it. See now.
When did you join the Strauss?
Uh... Let's see now. Uh... I don't know exactly. I'll tell you. The fella whose place I took was, uh... I think it was from England. Or Ireland. Joe Lyatt. Yeah.
Well, that's when he left.
And when he left New Orleans to go back home... Well, when I start sitting in with the group and I've been playing with him... I guess it must be close to a year now I've been playing.
Mm-hmm.
Uh... Having a lot of fun. Really, really like what I'm doing.
Wait a minute. He must have left to run May of last year.
This year.
May of this year, I mean.
Yeah. Yeah. You started playing, I believe, if I'll refresh your memory, you played trombone on a game you made in Cuba.

Yeah. Yeah. I forgot about it. Oh, I'm also a trombone. You didn't know that. That was in May, wasn't it? I think so, yeah. We went to Cuba with the group and Joe was still here. So I played the trombone on the trip. And I don't think I'll ever see my name up in lights, but I must say it sounded pretty good.
You made the gig anyway.
Yeah, I made it anyway, playing the trombone. I guess I'd have played the comb, the silk paper and comb to make that trip to Cuba, you know. I was willing to play anything.
What was it like down there?

That was a fine trip. What it was, it was a goodwill tour from the city of New Orleans. And they just happened to pick our group to go. And all the 11th quarters, we stayed in this Havana Hilton. That's one of the finest hotels in Cuba. And they really treated us like kings while we were there. We had a good time. We marched in a parade. They were in this, you see, they had this, oh, this big carnival of Cuba in Havana. And we marched in a parade and we had to use this blackface routine to represent a Negro funeral band. You see. The musicians were kind of half dead anyway, so we made a pretty good funeral band.
What tunes did you play as a funeral band?

Well, we played Didn't He Ramble, Just a Little While to Stay Here. We kind of jazzed up a version on Closer Walk with D. We played the Saints. and I think we more or less repeated the same tunes over and over, you know, parade stuff, you know.
Did you play a slow tune for a funeral, before the funeral?
No, we just went right into the marching routine, you know, we had to put more of a march beat to them, but those are supposedly Negro funeral tunes, that's the kind of stuff they played.
I mean, you played them as a, you were a coming back band.
A coming back band, that's it, yeah.
Well who was down there with you other than Joe?

Well, let's see, Joe was playing con-hit, Briss Jones was playing clarinet, Bill Lee played tenor sax, John Chaff, the regular banjo player, played tuba, and the regular drummer, Bob McIntyre, doubled on a banjo. The bass player played a bass drum, and the piano player played a snare drum, and I was the trombone. So all in all, it worked out pretty well, you know.
Well who's the bass player?
Bob Ice is the bass player, he's a regular bass player.
And who's the piano player?
Frank Delahousa plays piano.
And that's a regular bass, isn't it? Yeah. Well I call it a regular bass.

Well, I mean, we call it regular bass. No, this is a, this is a, he happened to get a few scraps of plywood, I think he got a genuine bass string, or two strings on it, he uses a couple of, what do they call these, hardware store buckles? Turnbuckles. Turnbuckles. And it produces a very effective sound, I mean, if you would close your eyes, you would swear you were listening to a genuine bass. Of course you can't look at this thing, but it sounds good.
Yeah. Very convenient too, it's got a hole cut in the side of it that he can carry all the accessories.
That's right, well, that's, I think that's how we managed to get our instruments from place to place, we just threw them right in the hole in the side of the bass, you see.
Why don't we add it, let me tell them about Willie Guitar and his bass is adoring it. Maybe you know the story better than I do, Paul.

I want to get this out. This guy Willie Guitar, who played bass and lived on Music Street, he's an old time bass man around here. I don't know, some old guys like I think Sal Mojada and Huey Hardy were talking one time to Sat, talking to me in the group and they said that Willie had a bass, had a door cut in the back of his bass, a hinged door, well concealed, and he'd go to a house party and he'd stand around and he'd see something he wanted, he'd pick out something real nice and after the party got real juiced up, nobody was paying any attention, he'd just sort of back up to whatever he wanted and open the door and stick it in there. So one night he saw a real expensive clock which had an alarm on it and he put that in there. Just as he was leaving the damn thing went off. They said he used to get a lot of stuff out of it later.
I've heard of case in a place but never bass in a place.
Well, back to the straws, how many days were you in Cuba you say?
We were down there five days. Five days? Yeah.
And how many jobs did you play?

Well, we went down there primarily for this parade, you see, this carnival parade. But while we were down there, the mayor, Mayor Morrison, had some sort of a party over there, you know, for his personal friends and he invited the band to play, see, so he used our band. All in all, I would say we made about three sessions other than the parade, see. We had a session going up in our hotel room one night and I think that was the best music we'd ever played. Of course nobody was there to listen to us but it really came through great, you know.
Were there any other bands from new audience down there?
Yeah, they had, Hector Fontana had a group over there and, oh this one boy was playing over at the dream room, not the dream room, a famous duo. Trumpet player?
Trumpet player.
Trumpet player, okay.
Murphy, Roy Liberto.

Roy Liberto, yeah, Roy Liberto. His group was over there. Incidentally, the other, Roy Liberto's group rode a float in the parade. They had some of the floats from the New Orleans Mardi Gras that was sent over there to go in this parade and Roy Liberto's group rode one of the floats. I don't know if Hector Fontana's band participated in the parade but they did some, you know, some of the extra parties and things like that. Our group, of course, had a march but all in all it was a real colorful parade. I think they had just about every country represented each, you know, country brought their own contingent or what would you call it. And it was a very colorful parade.
Did any of the other bands sound like jazz at all?

Uh, yeah, but I don't know, it seems to me that most, most of the, I don't know if I should be saying this, but most of the groups you hear now always seem to sneak in a modern touch somewhere along the line. You know, I mean, you just don't really hear that old, old brand of music. You hear jazz bands, you hear jazz tunes, but I don't know, maybe it's my ear, I don't know. But they just don't seem to have that crude sound as the old band had years ago, you know.
Well, I think the Englishmen have some of that.

Uh, speaking of Englishmen, there's this guy Chris Barber, I caught his show, you know, when he was at the auditorium. Boy, they, they were really hot stuff. They, now they produced pretty much of that real old sound.
Mm-hmm. How about any of the bands, not from your audience that were in Cuba, did they play any kind of, with a jazz feeling?

Well, uh, they were mostly, uh, school bands. Uh, I think, uh, one, one contingent over there was supposed to be a police band from some police department, I don't know where. But, uh, they played, uh, mostly parade and march stuff, you know. But, naturally, uh, representing New Orleans, we had to play jazz. We hardly knew any other music, see, we had to play jazz. Well, I, I should speak for myself then when I say hardly know any other music. I don't know hardly any other music. I just want to get the facts.
Facts.
Facts, man.
Let's see now. So, you came back and you didn't play with the straws again at all until May or so?

Uh, well, I, I think maybe I sat in twice with them playing trombone. One time I played, uh, I played the cornet. I played second cornet. Joe was playing first. And I, we tried to work up, uh, Oliver Armstrong get up, you see, with the first and second cornets. And, uh, well, after Joe left, well, of course, I had some big shoes to walk into, because, uh, Joe, I thought Joe, I tried to copy Joe's style. I think Joe was terrific. I mean, other people might have a different idea, you know, a different opinion of what they, what they would like to hear. But I thought Joe's stuff was great. Of course, his horn was always flat, but he was good. Could be, too, that vintage of horn he had. I think it was the first horn I'd ever made.
Yeah. When did you, uh, start playing spots with the straws?
Well, I guess, uh, it must have been about May. I think, uh, we had two jobs, uh, right, right after Joe left. We had these two jobs, and, uh, I played both of those.
What I mean is, you never substituted for Joe before he left.
Oh, no, no, no.
He always made all the jobs.

He always made all the jobs, yeah, unfortunately. Because I didn't want to get in and play, you know, more than I actually did. But, uh, I would go and listen to him, you know. I'd go up to Bruno's and listen to him play. And, uh, uh, uh, Briss, Briss Jones, the clarinetist, he played with this, uh, group we had up in Kenna years ago. You know, he sat in with us a couple of times. And, uh, he told John Chaff, he told John, he says, uh, he said, well, you know, Moose plays a con-ed. So, John asked me if I would like to sit in and play a tune with him, see. So, uh, oh, I think, uh, I think we played Hauna Society. And, uh, Bill Bailey, Milenburg, George. And, uh, John was pretty much pleased with the sound, you know. So, uh, he told me, he says, uh, you should keep practicing that horn, keep working on it, because Joe is going to be leaving us permanently. And, uh, we got to fill in, he says, and, uh, you know, the style of stuff you play is pretty much the same style that Joe plays. So, you know, you keep working with the horn and we'll have a spot for you in the groove. Well, I remember the first time I'd ever heard the Straws play, uh, it was at one of the jazz club meetings, uh, concerts, rather. And I told these fellas that I was with, I said, as far as I'm concerned, that's undoubtedly the most original sounding band in this city, bar none. He says, never dreamed that I'd ever have a chance to play with him, you know. And, uh, it all worked out.
Well, what do you play at other than Bruno's? What other places?

Well, uh, we make, uh, make a few, uh, fraternity house dances, uh, different luncheons. A little of everything, you know, the regular run of the mill jobs. Of course, nothing, uh, you know, another nightclub, but, uh, just enough to keep our hand in, you know, just to, just to keep busy. Paul, could you, uh, think of anything, you know, other types of jobs that the, the Straws would play? Uh, patio parties, things like that? For dancing at all?
They do, yeah. Well, they play a lot of dances.
Quite a few, yeah. Or places to be safe, dances.
Different organizations, different clubs, you know. But they, they're usually for, uh, in hard halls or at, uh, somebody's house almost.
Yeah, yeah, house parties, things like that, so yeah.
Uh, did you ever play out of town or other, well, we get to Vienna, but other than Cuba and Vienna?

Yeah, we, we made a, we made a job in, uh, what was it, Mobile? Wasn't it? Mobile, Alabama. They had, uh, oh, I think it was the, uh, opening of the debutante season or something, something to that effect, you know. And, uh, they hired the band to play over there. We went and played. Anywhere else? Uh, oh, I think we made two or three jobs in, uh, Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. So you keep pumping me, I could keep thinking of places now. Yeah.
Well, I'm pumping. I'm trying to think. Well, now what about these dance halls, rented halls? Where do you play at those? What are those?
Well, uh, it's some, some civic organizations, a lot of the fraternities. And, uh, well, I wouldn't know exactly how to, uh...
Well, I mean, say for example, do you ever play at the Woodmen of the World?

No, we've never, we've never played there. Not to my knowledge. I mean, you know, since I've been in the band, we've never played there. Uh, we made, uh, all two or three, uh, luncheons, uh, over at the country club, New Orleans Country Club.
Is that for dancing at the luncheon?
Well, they, they end up dancing, yeah. Yeah.
You accompany the orders or something?
Yeah.
Like on that chopstick?
Going at chopstick.
Something for the luncheon.

No, I was wondering. We also, uh, not to interrupt, but we also played for a breakfast one time. Uh, I can't see, uh, jazz with my scrambled eggs, you know, but they wanted, uh, they wanted a jazz band for a breakfast. And, uh, it was a 12.30 breakfast, 12.30 to 3.30, I believe. And, uh, gee, I mean, just waking up and going dancing, I can't see that, you know, but these people did.
Most of your job is uptown.
Yeah. Mm-hmm. What do you call it, the, uh, Uptown Social and Pleasure Club or something to that effect? Yeah.
Pretty much social.
Yeah.
I'm gonna keep pumping you because, uh, I think you-
Oh, I have to be led, you know.
I think, I think, I don't know, you might have played a job in Mobile, but you also played a job in another town in Alabama. I remember that. You don't remember that? Birmingham. Birmingham.
Yeah. Birmingham, yeah. I forgot that.
What kind of job was that?
Uh, gee, offhand, I can't remember.
What were you drinking that night?
Oh, ice water. That's all I drink when I play. I, I drink ice water.
Hmm. Why is that?

I don't know, uh, I, I, several times, uh, I sat on a bandstand and got pretty well tanked up, and, uh, I just lose all coordination. My lip and my finger won't work together, you know. So, I decided that was the time to get off of it, which I did. And now I'll drink ice water, maybe an occasional coke, but, uh, I strictly go in the ice water. Just to, you know, keep my throat and lips moist, you know.
How's this rail holding on? Five minutes. Um, let's see, Moose, maybe we should get on to Vienna now, huh? What happened? How'd you go to Vienna?

Um, this, uh, this thing I have a hard time explaining to most of my friends. See, right off the bat, you have to say it was a communist festival, you see. And, uh, of course the thing was dominated by communists. They invited the communists from the United States and all over the world. But, since this, uh, festival was given in a free country, see, Austria being a free country, this festival was given in Vienna, Austria. You see, so that, uh, we figured that as representatives of the free world, we should take this in, see, to kind of chip our side, you know. So, uh, we gave several street dances and, uh, we sold tickets and this and that and the other to get enough funds accumulated so we could go over there. Uh, we, incidentally, we paid our own way to go, see. So, uh, we went over there and, uh, we were, I guess you'd say the Raz and crew, you know, the heckling squad. We'll use that term. And, uh, they told us before we went that the people in Europe were having a jazz craze on right now. Apparently they don't get enough jazz over there, you see. Who does? Well, that's right, who does? So, uh, they decided to use our group. Well, the last straws made this trip, see. And, uh, just everywhere, every place we played, I mean, uh, the people accepted it so greatly, you know. It was, it was a great thing. I mean, it made us really feel like we were accomplishing what we went over to do. And, uh, we kinda threw a monkey wrench in the communist plans because the way they figured nobody would pay much attention to representatives of the free world, you see. Since it was their festival, they had the reins in their hands. They wanted everything to go their way, which it didn't. Cause, uh, they had lots of people that would just gather around the band and, you know, they wouldn't listen to the political speeches and whatnot. And that kinda, you know, that kinda burned them up a bit. Uh, I'll tell ya, uh, mahogany hall never sounds so good. Yeah. Uh, yeah, we kinda, kinda threw a wrench in their plans cause they expected things to go strictly their way. But, uh, naturally, members of the, uh, free world intervening the way they did, it kinda blew their works up, you know. And I'll tell ya this, uh, I think it will be the last time they will have a whole festival outside of the Iron Curtain. You see, usually the festival, the previous festivals, always in the, uh, Iron Curtain countries, the Russians have the reins in their hands. I mean, they make the rules, they play the game the way they wanna play it. They wanna play it. But since they came into a free country, they meant opposition, see, and they're not used to that. And, uh, all in all, uh, what we set out to do went over very well. You see, and, well, we naturally, all the members of the band got a great kick out of, you know, there's a lot of prestige. And we played in Europe. We made a tour of Europe, you know. And, uh, while we were over there, they had this, uh, fella who runs this International House of Jazz, they call it. Well, he made a contact with our group, and, uh, he wanted us to come play one night in his, uh, nightclub. Well, he's got a fabulous place, you should see this. So, uh, we went over and played this one night. And a lot of the people from the festival grounds had followed us over, plus a lot of his regular, you know, his regular customers. And, uh, he was so enthused with, uh, you know, with the response of the audience and this and that and the other that he wanted us to play for one month. He wanted to hire us for one month to stay over there. But seeing as we all had to come back to regular jobs and whatnot, you know, that was, that was impossible. But, uh, he told us, he says, uh, if y'all can make it back next year, he says, I'll pay all expenses and keep you all over here for, you know, one month. You can come play for the house, be the house band. Uh, about that time, uh, Louis Armstrong and, uh, Eliphas Jarrow, Oscar Pettiford, a whole crew of them were over there on tour. That's, that's when Louis got sick in Rome. Well, they were on their way back and we met them in this International House of Jazz, you see. So we just had one big ball, you know. And, uh, autographs, autographs, we're going to dine with that. I think it's the first time I've signed my autograph, you know. Made me feel good, you know, made me feel important.
Well, did you cut Louis or did he cut you?

No, uh, unfortunately, Louis had to stay in Rome. He wasn't up to par, you know. He was taking a solo in Rome. He was in the hospital, I believe. But you did, those guys sat in with you some of them over there? Well, uh, we played, uh, we played as, uh, uh, Bill Bailey and Ella did a vocal for us. And, uh, Oscar Pettiford, uh, he's a terrific bass man. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Oscar Pettiford now. We're talking about him.

Yeah well, Pettiford didn't, I don't know, he didn't particularly like that style of music we were playing. He plays more on the progressive side, you know. But you really have to appreciate the musicianship. The guy really slaps the bass, man. He's great.
And who else came and sat in?

Well, that was about the only ones that were there at the time. You see, I don't know, I guess it's sort of traditional. This house of jazz, any time a famous musician or a celebrity passes through, they should stop in this place and sign the book. So, it just so happens that we were in there when these people, Pettiford and Ella came through. And, you know, being in a place like that, you just get to see all the celebrities, all the greats and whatnot. Incidentally, this fellow that ran the place, his name was Fatty George. He's an Austrian. And he really goes for the old New Orleans jazz. I mean, that's the only kind of music he really took an interest in, you see. And on the walls in his place, he's got life-size pictures of Baiderbeck playing with, I think it was Tommy Darcy. On another wall, he's got Bum Johnson and a group that he was playing with. And on another wall, he's got the Eureka Brass Band. I mean, the wall is just covered with these life-size pictures, you see. And so many of the people over there, you know, the people that really went to his place, that like jazz, they've heard of New Orleans. But to them, it was more of a legendary place. They never actually thought they'd get to see people and hear people directly from New Orleans playing music over there, see. So, we played and we made a week, I always say over that week. So, Fatty had pictures made of our group. Of course, not life-size, but they were very big pictures and he put them on the wall next to all the greats, you see. And, I mean, you know, it kind of does something for you. It makes you feel like you're somebody, you know. And, well, the people over there were autograph hounds. They went for autograph. I must have signed my name about 50 times while I was over there. You know, little things like that that make you feel good about playing, you know. All I know, we really, really had a fine. You see, well, ten days we stayed at this festival. Now, we were playing, oh, maybe three, maybe four times a day during the festival, see. Every time they'd have a rally going over here, they'd call a band. And they might have one over here, they'd call a band again. So, we would, you know, we were keeping pretty active. Plus, our little job we had in town every night, see, when we were playing over at Fatty's. So, well, like I say, the festival lasted ten days. And after the ten days were up, well, we sort of took off on more or less a vacation. See, we went on our own then. John Chaff went to Paris. Bill and Carol Lee went to Munich. They stayed over at Carol's brother's house. And Bob Ice, and myself, and JJ. I'm at a loss for his last name right now. Joyce. JJ Joyce. We went to Salzburg. And we went to this little mountain resort, the Zolom Z, they call it. And we lived it up there. We had quite a time. You playing? No. Well, as a matter of fact, we left our instruments in Vienna. We left them in Vienna. And on the way back through, we picked them up. And, well, when we went back to pick these instruments up, we made two tapes in Fatty's place. You know, during the, oh, it must have been midday. Nobody was in the place. And, you know, the tape itself had good effect. It didn't have any background noise and whatnot. And if I'm not mistaken, I think Bob Ice might have this tape. And to my way of thinking, I don't know, they might have a different opinion on it, but I think that was as good as our group ever sound. You know, all the while we won this trip, see. And it was terrific. I wish I could come by this tape one day. I'd like to just listen to the stuff again, you know. What did Bill Lee play? Bill played clarinet. Well, he's clarinet and sax, man. But on this Vienna trip, he played strictly clarinet. Briss Jones didn't make the trip, see. Bill's wife played piano, because Della Husa couldn't make the trip. I think he was on duty with the National Guard at the time. So, Carol Lee played piano. Bill Lee played the clarinet. I played cornet. John played the banjo. J.J. played the drums. Ice played bass. And we picked up a trombone player while we were over there. A fellow by the name of William Mirwald. He's an Austrian. And, well, you'd swear this guy was born in New Orleans, Austria. He could play a tailgate trombone. It was out of this world, you know. And he promised to come over here. He wanted to come to New Orleans and get back with the group. And, of course, he must have thought we were playing full time, you see. I mean, he couldn't quite make a living out of something like that, you know, just off and on.
You don't know how to spell that name, huh?
I think it is M-E-E-R-V-A-L-D. I think that's the way he spelled it. William Mirwald.
We'll get it from Ice.

Bob Ice should have it. Yeah, I think he has his address and all, you know. He's gonna keep contact with him. Incidentally, John enrolled Willie as a correspondent member in New Orleans Jazz Club, you know. So that's one more finger reaching out across the sea, you know. So Willie's a member now, I think.
Let's get all the men in the band straight while we're talking about all that. Who was with the band when you first joined?

Well, when I first joined, well, like I said, I took Joe's play, see. Okay, I'll start from that time. Yeah. Well, I was playing cornet. Bruce Jones was playing clarinet. Bill Lee was playing sax. Frank Della Hussi was playing piano. J.J. Joyce, drums. Bob Ice, bass. But Bill has swapped from his alto to a soprano sax. He plays soprano sax now. It's pretty effective. It's got a good sound. Now then we'll get different people sitting in with us, you know. Oh, the trombonist. We got a boy by the name of Archie Rogers playing trombone. He's very good. And once in a while, different people come and sit in just to, you know, be in on the session, you know. As many people want to come over, we're always glad to have them, you know, because I know they just enjoy sitting in as much as I enjoy sitting in when I first went to play with the group, you know.
Bob Havens, I've seen him.
Bob Havens. Bob Havens sat in with us. Bill Dodson sat in with us. At one time, I think Johnny Wiggs had sat in with the group. Bob Havens. But that was while Joe was still here, I believe.
You mean Glenn Dodson?
Bob Havens. No, Bill.
Oh, the clarinet player.
Bob Havens. Yeah, he's a clarinetist, yeah.
He's a trombone player.

Let's see. Bob Havens. Bob Havens. Well, there's several students from Tulane. Well, naturally, a lot of the people in this place are from Tulane and Newcomb. You know, they come to the place where we play. And once in a while, one of those will get up on the bandstand and you'd be surprised what some of them can do. You just don't know they're jazz musicians until you hear them, you know, get on the bandstands. And, well, two or three times already, well, since I've been with the group, I've heard some of these students get up there and play with the band. And they're great. What style do they play for students? Well, it's hard to try to detect exactly who they copied off of, you see. But, I mean, they just have a way of playing Dixieland jazz or New Orleans jazz, you know. Old style?
Old style.

Old style clarinet, yeah. Old style piano. We had a fellow sat in with us just this past Sunday. I don't know his name. I don't know where he came from, but he was a pretty good pianist. And we did a version on Millenberg. And, I mean, this guy could really pawn a piano.
He sort of sounded like Duncan and Palmisano, you know, those guys.

I'm sorry I didn't catch his name. He'd probably come back up again. Well, just that type of music attracts them, they will be back, see, and they're going to want to play again. We're always glad to have them play.
But, now, that was not a young student type, so you'd expect him to play Old Style. He wasn't, no. Well, I mean. I'm surprised that there's that many students that play Old Style.

Well, surprised. You see, the way I figure this, the older people heard this music once before, and it's familiar to them. The newer people, the younger people, hadn't heard it, and it's something all together new to them, so that attracts them. And, well, the surprise is it is. I mean, some of these youngsters, I'd say, 18, 19 years old, can play some of these older tunes. Law knows they were way before these kids' time, but they know the tunes, you know, just as if they were brought up around the tune. They say, and they can play them.
Well, I know too much mustard, and I certainly wasn't around when that was popular.

Well, that's the same with me. Some of these tunes, I remember, well, my mother used to hum them, you see. Of course, at the time, I didn't know the name of the tune, but over a period of years, you know, you start fooling around, fooling around. You say, well, this might sound right, and you'll add this to the tune.
And before you know it, you actually piece that whole tune, and you're playing it just the way it was originally meant to be, you know.

Well, myself, I speak for myself, playing by ear like that, I mean, I have to rely on that, see. That's the only way I can play it. I have to hear it. If I heard it once before, I could play it, you know. But, it's, I'm at a disadvantage, of course, not being able to read music. I always said I would give my ride on if I could read music. But, I just have to rely on what I hear right now. It's kind of, you know, that old saying, you can't teach old dog new tricks. You know.
I want to get the band, as it's changed now. Have you had any substitute drummers in since JJ started?

Well, the original drummer with the group was Bob McIntyre. And, well, a couple months back, Bob's wife had a baby. And, naturally, Bob had to give more time to his family, you know, and he couldn't get out the way he wanted to make these jobs at night. And, then, John Joyce, JJ started playing with us. And, from what I hear, I don't know, it might just be a rumor. But, JJ Joyce has won the Trap Drumming Championship at Mississippi State for about four years in a row. Now, I don't know how authentic that is, but he is very good. He's a very good drummer. He's a young boy, I mean, he, but he, uh, he just happened to catch that old New Orleans style of drumming, you know. He's not a cymbal player. He's just a sophomore, isn't he? I think so. He's a, he's a dental student. I might get him to make a bridge for me, you know. I need teeth something awful right now. And, uh, a trumpet player without teeth is like a barber without hands, you know.
Well, old Barnaback, that's you.
It's more like bunk, huh? They bought bunk teeth, maybe they'll buy me some teeth. Well, I might get lucky one day.
Uh, let's see now. Have you had any changes? Your trombone player didn't go to Europe with you. No. You had the same trombone player all along, you had the same clarinet player, except he didn't go.
He didn't go, no.
Let's see, who else might have changed? I don't think anybody has.

Well, no, it's, uh, it's been pretty much the same, same group, you know. Uh, maybe one, uh, one fellow might sit in for another one Sunday, you know. But we keep pretty much around the same bunch of guys that had been playing, you know.
But you don't have cymbal drummers, huh?

No, he, uh, he beats a real, well, I think this boy could get by on just a snare drum and a bass drum alone. Uh, I mean, it has more of that parade sound. In a parade, you didn't have all these, uh, all these cymbals and all the wood chocks and whatnot. And, uh, of course he does know how to play them, but, uh, in this particular style of music we play, uh, he relies mostly on his snare and bass drum.
But you don't go for all that, uh, stuff with high notes and fast tempos?

Uh, well, no, you see, that, uh, I'll tell you something. Uh, I've always been able to play in one key only, which was B flat. Everything I played had to be played in B flat, say. But, well, since I've been playing with this group naturally, you got some, some pretty good, uh, musicians in the group. These guys really know that stuff. And over a period of a year or so, uh, I think they taught me to play in just about every, you know, every key. But, uh, I try to minimize my stuff by keeping it more on a lower scale and try to get up in the, in the atmosphere, you know. Uh, I, I, I like to play in a lower register, but, uh, it's not always effective, you know, in some tunes. So you have to get high.
Uh, but what I mean is the, the general atmosphere of the band is not that of Bourbon Street musicians.
Uh, no, no.
You're not aiming for the same thing.

Well, you know, most of the bands, I don't know, maybe, maybe I shouldn't be saying this, but to me, most of the bands you're here on Bourbon Street now, uh, they all seem to get a modern trend in their music. The drummers will rely strictly on their cymbals. The trumpet players have to do these soaring notes, you know, all this high, all the high playing. And they more or less modernize it. Of course, it's still supposed to be the old tune, but they kind of modernize it, see. And, uh, I like the old jazz for what the old jazz was. See, nothing fancy. It was just, just good pure music.
Well, do you have many records yourself?

Uh, I, I have, uh, I guess I have about 30 or 40 records of my own, you know. And, uh, I think most of the stuff I might have learned right off those records, you know, listening to the records and just pick it up.
That's LPs or 78s of them?

LPs. You see, uh, well, like I said before, uh, I like Bunk Johnson. I like Big Spider-Bank. I like King Oliver. So what I do is try to combine all that three styles together and maybe I'll come up with one of my own, who knows.
I like to play their stuff, you know. Any other trumpet players you can think of from your records?
Uh, I like, uh, I like Johnny Wigg. I like the way Johnny Wigg plays. He has a simple pure style. I like that. Uh, he, uh, let's see, I'm trying to think of this, this other, was it Emmett Hardy?
They talk about him.
He sounds pretty much like a, a recording I have of Emmett Hardy. Their stuff sounds pretty much the same, you know, and I like that. I like that, that style.
I don't think you have a record of Emmett Hardy. Was it Emmett Hardy? I don't think he made any records I've ever issued.
You know? Well, I might be wrong. I'm a, maybe, maybe it's something I'd overheard that their styles were... Yeah. I'm pretty sure, I'm pretty sure it's, uh, it's something on Emmett Hardy.
Well...
You got me thinking, um, I have to think about it.
Yeah. If you got an Emmett Hardy record, let me know. It should be worth a couple of thousand at least. Well good, I'll sell it. It could be though, you know, those things turn up.
It's just like a, like a bowling recording. They tell me that's worth a little money if you can find one, huh? Yeah. Did he ever do any recording? Supposed to have.
Even Hardy made home recordings and nobody could find them. Buddy Petit made home recordings.
We were talking about Jolly Roll too. You listening to a lot of Jolly Roll?

Uh... Well, uh, I had one or two records with the, uh, the Hot Peppers, Red Hot Peppers. And, uh, this fellow that plays Cornet in their group, uh, a guy by the name of George Mitchell. He was, uh, he was a good Cornetist. I liked his style. And, uh, I'll say once before, he appears to be a musician that might have come from one of these orchestra pits. He plays that type of stuff, you know. He's good. He's really good.
I heard you play something one time on Lillingberg. It sounded like Paul Morell, but you said you never heard any of Paul Morell's stuff, huh?
No, no, no. That's, uh, oh, you're talking about that first note on Lillingberg, that growl, huh?
Yeah, all the lyrics.
I don't know. I thought it might have sound good then, so I just used it, see? See, I have to invent my stuff as I go along, so yeah.
Now you play Cornet or trumpet? Cornet.

No. Oh, years ago, well, the first instrument I bought was a trumpet. And, uh, I played it quite some time. And, well, when I got to playing with the Last Straw, I was naturally being supposed to be an old jazz group. They use the old type of instrument, so I went and traded my, uh, trumpet in for a Cornet. The Cornet being the old type of instrument, it fits in with that, uh, with that set-up, see?
Can you tell any difference in the tone or anything?

Uh, I think, uh, well, from what I can understand, I think a Cornet is supposed to be more of a solo instrument. You see, uh, your trumpet, your trumpet, uh, might have a sweeter tone, higher pitch, but a Cornet, a Cornet's just a solo instrument. It's just a big brass instrument. It makes a lot of noise, see? It's supposed to be the lead instrument, and you, I guess you're supposed to hear this one louder than any other, huh?
Do you like, which tone do you like the best, really, if you had your choice?

Uh, how do you mean, uh, which, which tone? The trumpet or the clarinet? Oh, I like, I like, uh, I like the Cornet. I like the Cornet. So, you know, you take, uh, these fellows that play, you know, strictly the sweet dance music, uh, they would have to use trumpet. See, it's that, that type of instrument where the Cornet's, uh, more of a, what you'd say, uh, something that would be used in a brass band or a marching band or something of that type, see? He was a cornet.
It's funny, Kid Howard would have switched back to Cornet, too, you know?
Did he switch back? I know, uh, I have, uh, a recording horn by George Lewis, and on the, uh, jacket, on the album jacket, they show, uh, Kid Howard playing a trumpet. Yeah. He's got a trumpet.

But he's back on the Cornet, and you even see modern guys now going to the Cornet, like, I heard Melvin last year, uh, I think it was Friday night, uh, at, uh, the jazz room on Dolphin Street, you know? Yeah, at the corner. And, uh, he was playing Cornet.

Well, uh, I was, uh, fortunate enough to catch, uh, Wilbert DiPerry's group in New York. And, uh, Sidney DiPerry has both a trumpet and a Cornet. He hangs them both on his music stand. Now, whichever tune they play, the type of tune he plays, that, you know, that's the decided fact as to which instrument he will use. If they play the real old New Orleans, uh, Mark stuff, he takes his cornet. If he plays something, maybe more of a, uh, a dance tune, he'll use his trumpet.
Hmm. Well, one more thing I wanted to ask you about was that compliment you told me you got.

Oh, yeah. Uh, yeah, it seems that just before we went to York, we were playing a street dance in order to raise funds for our trip, see? So, in this particular neighborhood that we were playing is, well, it's predominantly a colored section. So, they had one old colored fella, he was hanging by the rope, you see? We had this area roped off and he was hanging back there by the rope, doing a jig and a dance out in the street, see? So, when we had an intermission, I walked over to the rope and was talking to him, and he told me, he says, uh, you know, he says, for white fellas, y'all play the darkest music I ever heard. And naturally, we are trying to reproduce that old Negro sound, and to me, that was a great compliment, you know, because that's what we want to do. Yeah, he says, for a white group, y'all make the darkest music I ever heard.
Oh, what did that guy say to you at the, what was it, the Yacht Club or the Country Club? Uh, that guy, the waiter comes up to you and plays you a high compliment, remember? The guy from Cuba?
He said, I sound just like, uh, Big Chief, huh?
Oh.
He said, I play that just like, uh, Jacare. I play that part in that tune just like Jacare. Jacare. Jacare.
Jack Carey.
Uh, Jack Carey. Uh-huh.
That guy had come over from Cuba when?
So real early. 1918.

Um, well, you know, it's surprising how many of these people that come from other places know so much about, uh, you know, about, uh, Dixie Lounge. Uh, when we were over in Europe, uh, all these people would come up to us and they'd ask us if we knew, uh, George Lewis, uh, do we know Lawrence Marrera, do we know Al Hurt, and, uh, for the sake of a joke, I told them, I said, well, I taught Al Hurt to play a horn. And, uh, golly, I'd never seen Al, uh, I wish I had the opportunity to meet him. I like him, you see, but I'd never seen, I'd never seen Al play. And, uh, these people just thought that was something, you know, until I had to let them on that I was just joking, you know. I don't think there's another Al Hurt in the country, boy.
Well, who, who did you hear over there? Did you listen to any bands on your way back?

Uh, well, we just, uh, had the opportunity to catch, uh, De Parry's band in New York, but over there, I mean, uh, uh, all the groups that were sent over there were all modern jazz groups. We were the only, uh, Dixieland group, you know, on this tour, see. Everything else was, uh, modern jazz. Most of the, uh, people from over there, the Austrians themselves, they, they have bands in the different nightclubs and all, and they all play modern jazz. So, uh, to hear Dixieland was something different for them, you know. I had one fella tell me that during the war that, uh, Hitler outlawed, uh, jazz. He would not let the people listen to jazz because there was only one thing, you know, that they should adore, and at the time it was him. And anybody caught listening to jazz records or anything that they, you know, took a particular interest in, they were jailed, you see. So now these people are loose and free, they can, you know, they can listen to and say what they want, see. Uh, I tell you, they, they really, really liked listening to the music. Every place we played, a place was just packed, you know. So, oh, golly, we had, we had a chance of playing, uh, castles. We played in palaces. I, I guess those little walls never figured they'd ever be listening to Dixieland jazz, huh?
Where was this, at Vienna, that area you played in, castles? Yeah, mm-hmm.

Yeah, we went to this, uh, all this great palace, I forget the name of it. But, uh, they had, uh, some kind of benefit on for the, uh, Austrian free youth. And they used our group, they asked us to play. And they also asked us, there was a Negro boy, a fella by the name of Lorenz Graham. He accompanies himself with a guitar, he sings folk music, you know. And, uh, they had, uh, the Stan K. Quintet, that was a modern group. And, uh, we had about, I guess about five, five different groups that put the show on, see. And, uh, we played in a castle, huh, or a palace. And, that's, uh, that's something out of the ordinary. I mean, you just don't play in palaces every day, you know.
Well, over there, who sent these groups, uh, from America?

Well, uh, you have a, a large communist following in New York. And you have a large communist following in Chicago, you see. So, uh, what happened, we were able to latch on with one of the, uh, two big groups, like I said, which was New York and Chicago. We were able to latch on with the, uh, the New York group. We went over with them, see. And, uh, well, like I say, this thing being in a free country, I mean, they couldn't very well put us out, you see. So, uh, we got over there and, uh, we were, we were the official heckling squad.
Did the, uh, communists provide you places to play value over there?

Uh, well, uh, what happened, uh, the living quarters we had and the accommodations were terrible. I mean, none of us, uh, you know, were too happy over the setup over there. But, uh, we figured if we could stick it out for, for ten days, we got it with, see. Now, I think they arranged these bad plays as far as with the intentions of us getting fed up and leaving, you see. That's what they, they couldn't very well tell us to get out, but they didn't want us to stay, you see. So, when they seen that that wouldn't work, uh, well, they, they just about put us under all kind of conditions you could think of like that, say. But when they seen that wouldn't work, then they resorted to violence. I mean, they were having street fights and riots, you know, all the time. Uh, but none of this affected the band in any way because we went over strictly as musicians, not as a political group. You see, we had no connections with the, with politics whatsoever, you see. And, uh, half of the time, uh, the communists and the non-communists hardly knew which side we were on, you see. I mean, they just came for the sake of listening to the music, you know. And the last few days of the festival, of course, they found out that, you know, we were, we were non-communish, you know. But, uh, the way we refer to them, uh, we call the communist Indians and the non-communist the cowboys. And whenever we would talk within the band, you know, we, we'd refer to them as the cowboys and Indians. So, if there was any bad guys listening, they didn't know what was going on, you see. And it worked, though. It was the cowboys and the Indians. That's funny. You see, we, we didn't want to get involved in politics in any way, you see. We didn't go over there for political purposes. We went over to play music and to have the prestigious same we played in Europe, you see. And, uh, I mean, it's a great thing, you know. It's not every, everybody gets a chance to go to Europe and play music, you know.
Well, jazz is a little bigger than all that jazz. Yeah.
You know, anyway. Well, I tell you, I never thought I would ever travel around the world on a stage. I mean, I got to go to Cuba, went to Europe, all on the oil horn. Mobile, they say no.
Yeah, yeah.
Been to slide down yet? No, uh, they tell me we're going to play at the snake farm next week.
Well, you had to learn some special numbers like that. Snake rag.
Snake rag, yeah.
Yeah. Defused it.
Louis Armstrong did it. Yeah. Well, uh, anyway.
Oh, well, who was fighting? There wasn't any musicians fighting at all, huh? No.

Well, you see, uh, actually what happened, they, uh, they had, uh, a group from, uh, Israel. They had a group from Palestine. They had a group from Italy. You know, all the countries were represented, see. And, uh, naturally most of them were common, you see. Now, the true Russians themselves, the ones directly from, uh, Moscow and, uh, Leningrad and all, they stayed on a houseboat out in the Danube River. They didn't come on to festival grounds at all because they didn't want to have anybody say, well, the Russians caused this, you see. They wanted to keep as clear as possible, you see. In other words, let their little strong-on boys go out and do the work, you know. Uh, oh, that reminds me, speaking of this Italian group, they had a group over there, they called them the Italian New Orleans Jazz Band, so help me.
I know the manager, I think, the brother of the manager. Of this group?

Yeah. Well, anyway, uh, I don't know, it might have just been coincidence, but every place we played, these guys, these guys showed up right behind us. They were on the program, see. And every place we played, they were right behind us. And, uh, when they actually found out, well, we told them, we were from New Orleans, you see. And they thought we were handing them a line just like they handed everybody else a line in an Italian New Orleans Jazz Band, you see. But, uh, I mean, they were pretty well shocked when they actually found out that we were directly from New Orleans and we'd come there to play New Orleans music, you see. So I think they kind of hung around with us to pick up as much stuff as they could, you know, in our style of playing or what we do. On a bandstand or something like that, you know. But, uh, I mean, they were really amazed when they found out that we actually were from New Orleans.
Well, are they a communist group?

Yeah, they were with the communist group from over there. Mm-hmm. Communist Italy. Uh, we were playing, uh, one in this place. And, uh, it was in this big mess hall, you see, a big, uh, big dining room. And, uh, we were actually scheduled for this program, you see. They called us over to play that night. So in the middle of our session, here comes a bunch of people carrying flags and stars and doves, you know, and sticks, you see. And they come in stomping, you know. So naturally, uh, the people that were around the band went over to say, Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
We're talking about that communist parade that came in.

Yeah, so right in the midst of one of our tunes, I forget just exactly what tunes we're playing, so these feet stompers come in carrying the stars and the sickles and all the trimmings that go with the communist rallies. You see. So we figured we'd stop and let them have the show a while, you see, so we figured we were going to compromise. We'd take a turn to play a tune and let them do something, and we'd play and let them do something. But it didn't work that way. They just wanted the whole show for themselves, see, so they'd start making with these Russian dancers, you know, where you fold your arms and squat and you dance, you see.
Kazatska.

Is that what you call it? Well, anyway, when this group comes marching in, the people left the band and went and surrounded these people and see what they had to show. So we seen that they weren't going to give us another break to play, you see. They just wanted to dominate this whole thing. In other words, they wanted us to get out, you know, in not so many words. So they sing in one of their anthems. Oh, man, they got all kinds of anthems. So they sing in one of their anthems, and by some twist of luck, we were able to pick up the key that they were singing in, and we start playing this thing along with them, you see. Not that we had ever heard it before. We just start playing the thing they're singing. So the people got a bang on it, they start cheering for the band, and they all came back over to the band again, see. So these characters start throwing stale bread and water at us. They seen that we had the group coming back to us, and that kind of riled them up, you see. I mean, it wasn't supposed to be that way. It wasn't planned that way. So they start throwing this bread and water at us. So if these guys would have realized how hungry I was, I think they'd have threw a little ham and cheese with it, too, because, boy, they fed us lousy over there, you know. But we swayed the crowd back to the band, and the culprits were punished by the ground police, you know, the people that were circulating through the crowds to keep law and order. They had two or three little fellas from Pakistan that were picked up. They were the instigators, you see. They were the ones that started all this business. But we got back to playing our music again, and we swayed the crowd back to us. And I mean, that's a general pattern of what happened all along. We would play the crowd. It would all come back to us, you see. So I can truthfully say, for what we went over that far, we accomplished what we had to do, you see.
That's really tricky. You're playing their own number. You sort of answer a fool with his father, you know.

You see, it was just one of those things. I mean, either one of us had ever heard this song before, you know, had no idea what it was. You just feel like a certain note should follow a certain note when you're playing along like that. See, it just falls into a pattern, you know. And we picked this tune up and just played it as if it was written for our band. And the people really got a charge out of that. They probably figured that we actually knew this tune, you know. But either one of them had never heard it before.
What tunes did they request most often?

Every time we would play, we'd have a hundred requests for Dr. Jazz. And unfortunately, the lead man didn't know Dr. Jazz. I know it now, though. And if ever, oh, we got a letter. They just sent us a letter. They want us to go to Rome next year for a similar DLC. And you can bet if we go to Rome, I will play Dr. Jazz until I'm blue in the face. I know it now.

I have to give you that guy's name over there that I know. His name is Claude Cock. K-O-C-H. He sounds like a Frenchman and a German, but he's in Rome last I heard from him. He was over here in Biloxi training for the Italian Air Force. And he bought a lot of my records. He wanted to get old, you know, kid shots records and stuff like that. I was starving, I think, at the time. I told him, $30 worth of records.

Well, we got this letter. I mean, they want us to go to Rome now. Well, it's going to be a similar deal. And we also supposed to go to Washington, D.C., February 27th for the, they got this Congressional Carnival Ball over there. And we supposed to play for that. So we keep an active just enough to, you know, keep in shape, you know. Do you rehearse? Huh? Do you rehearse? Well, I'll tell you, there's rumor that we're getting ready to make a record for the Louisiana Historical Society. Now, this, this fella made a contact with us. He figured that our groups still sound like one of the real old, original New Orleans bands. So that's why he decided on using our groups. And they want to, they want us to record, I think it's something like 12 tunes. And we have been rehearsing this past week. We're going to start rehearsals so we can get these tunes down to the note, you know, so there will be no flaws.
It contacts through Bill Cray, you know. I didn't know that. I didn't know that.
Yeah, he's the one that tipped him off. Really?
It's the Louisiana Folklore Society. Is that what it is?

Well, I tell you, there's business going over my head all the time. I just know that I should show up when we have an engagement. Yeah. I'll leave all the figure into Chaff and Ice. They have been making most of the arrangements for us and whatnot. But I just work for the bunch, you know.
Yeah, Bill used to sit in too. He's in that one. Bill Cray, yeah. He did sit in already, yeah. Raymond played a few jobs, you see.

Well, that was before, Raymond played, I think while Joe was still here. Raymond, Raymond Burke played with the group. He hadn't played since I've been in the group, but I would like very much, you know, the opportunity to play with him, you know. I stopped over at Raymond's shop pretty regular and looked at some of these weird instruments he has in there. And I seen one evening I was passing, coming home from work, and he called me over and showed me this trumpet he had. With a lot of copper tubing on it and whatnot. So he played, he was playing a sort of thing, looked like a clarinet. And I was playing this trumpet. We were sitting right out there, right in front of his shop, right on the street. And we had a jam session, just the two of us sitting there, you know. And he's got some of the weirdest looking things there. He made a trombone, I think, with a lead pipe and funnels and this and that and the other. He's got a trombone.
That's got a tenor mouthpiece and a, for a bell it's got a plunger.
Yeah, that's right.
Two pieces of pipe. Yeah, I know that one. That's right, that's the thing. That's it. Paul's played that. He calls it a plunger phone or something. Yeah. I like to call it a plumber's nightmare.

Well, I don't know, I guess this thing that he's got with this trumpet with all the copper tubing, it looks more like a trumponet. You know, it looks like it might be part clarinet and part trumpet. You can't tell what it is.
Yeah. And then what's that thing that looks like a clarinet, it's got a cane reed or something on it. You've never seen it has a clarinet mouthpiece then he'd just have a piece of cane with it.
Yeah. With the holes. It's all bamboo flute. Mm-hmm. With a clarinet mouthpiece on it. It's ringing or something.

I stopped around there once and I wanted to get a tuba from him. I thought maybe he'd have an old tuba for sale, you know. But he didn't have anything that even resembled the tuba. He's got quite an interesting shop. You go in there, you could spend a day just looking. Of course you don't have far to go. You could spend a day trying to get in.
You spend a day trying to get in.
You spend a day trying to get in, that's right. But he's got a little bit of everything. There's only one Raymond.
One Raymond. There will be another one. There will be another one. What would you say the main difference between European jazz fans and American jazz fans?

I really couldn't detect that much of a difference. In Europe, you have more people flocking around to see what's going on. Because, well, like they say, they're stars for jazz over there. And naturally, wherever you set up, you get a bigger following. But they react the same way as the people react right here, you know. I mean, they know it's a happy music and they're having a happy time listening to it, you know. Clapping and whistling and whatnot.
Let's see, who comes up there at Bruno's? Now, when I'm up there, I see people I know from around school. Tulane, Newcomb.

Yeah, well, I would say, well, the name of the place is Bruno's College Inn. So, naturally being right up in this section of town around Tulane and Newcomb, you have a lot of students from Newcomb and Tulane that go over there, you see. And during the school year, well, we'll play from 5 to 7. You see, it's pretty early in the evening. And from what I can understand, I think most of the students have to get back in dormitories at certain times. So we don't want to confine too much of that time to, you know, stay in over there. But we get a pretty good group in every Sunday afternoon. After school closes, well, we play later hours. We'll start at 7 and play till 9. And then you'll find you have more of an older group of people that come in to listen, you know. But during school time, we'll play from 5 to 7 on a Sunday, give them a chance to go listen to music. Then if they want to go catch a show downtown, they still got time, you see.
At parties, do you play for like young and old or like?

Young and old like, yeah. You have, I don't know, when you're playing that kind of music, the old just automatically turn young. So I guess you're playing for all young people really. Yeah, that's right.

I heard that Birmingham job, you couldn't remember anything about it, but from what I remember, that I was told, I think a girl who goes to school here, or had gone to school here, had a bunch over at Bruno's and she knows ice. And she had gotten her father to put up a pretty good bundle to bring the band up there for two hours and they followed a regular dance that they had at their house, didn't they?

Yeah, yeah. Yeah, that's right. Well, again too, now that goes back to the business angle, see, which I'm not too, too familiar with, but that's how we got to make the trip over there. Incidentally, we started playing, must have been, what time? 12, 12 o'clock, 3 o'clock, it was a ridiculous hour we started. But before this, they had a nice dance band there. I mean, these guys were strictly, you know, reading musicians that were very good. And one of the fellas, the guy who fronted his band was a trumpet man, and he played with Charlie Spivak's orchestra. And he had a bunch of young musicians and they played, you know, all nice dance music. But after they had knocked off, after their job was over, they went and asked the lady who was running the thing if it would be alright if they would stay and listen to the New Orleans band play. And she gave them permission to stay. So they all cluttered around the back of the bandstand and they actually went wild. I mean, you know, they said, well, how can you guys do this without having music in front of you? You know, they couldn't get over that. We're making this stuff up almost as we go along, you see. And they were pretty well pleased with the, you know, with the resolve. That is kind of hard to understand. Well, like I tell people, they want to know, what is jazz supposed to be? Or what is Dixie Landon? Dixie Landon. Now, the way I look at it, it's each musician is playing a solo simultaneously. You see, in other words, you're making your stuff up as you go along. In other words, these guys actually playing a solo together.
Well, do you think the guys listen to each other while they're playing?

Um, I do. I don't know. I guess most everybody does. But, uh, when, uh, either a trombone or a clarinet will take a solo. Well, I sit there and I really listen to it and I enjoy what I hear, you know.

Well, now you say, last Sunday when I was there, I heard you play something, a lick, and then I heard Archie adapt part of that, you know, into his lick right after that, you know. But just some little variation on the tune, you know, and he worked that right into his, just answered you, you know. Yeah. Like, you know, it's obvious the guys in the band, all together, even though they're all playing solo.

Well, I think, uh, if you play as a group long enough, you almost know what the other guy's thinking. And you can do that same thing, say, uh, follow him, uh, maybe take the lead, you know, work at the guys first, or like that. Uh, most, uh, well, I don't know, uh, not being, uh, a reading musician, or really knowing that much about music. I would think that while one guy is playing a solo, a regular musician would be counting time. See, he knows how many beats have to go in a measure, and he knows when this other guy's solo is just ready to end, see. Now, with me, it's not like that. I don't know how to count time. So I just, you know, I come in when I think the solo is over, we see. Like, when one guy's playing a solo, I think he's finished, and I'll come in. I might be wrong on that now, but I've always had that impression that while one fellow's playing a solo, a regular musician is counting the timing. You know, keeping time, or counting how many measures. Well, some many men do that during the symphony, but... Well, uh, they'll show me a sheet of music. I'm lucky I can read the name of the tune, much less the notes on it.
You didn't study music in school at all.
No, no, no. Well, I made a statement. Huh? Pardon me?
Didn't you tell me one time that you played the flute once?

Well, uh, I didn't take lessons. I had a flute. And, uh, at the time, I was listening to, uh, well, a lot of classical music. And I heard something, I said, boy, I'd like to know how to play this. So I had this flute. I rented a flute. And I learned how to play, uh, all the walls of the flowers and some of the stuff from Pete and the Wolf. Uh, I can't think of the names of it. But anyway, I just like the sound, so I'll play. Well, that's the same thing I do with the trumpet. I like the sound, and I'll play it, see? I mean, if I went and bought this trumpet, and if I didn't learn how to play it, I was just out of money, you see? So, it was either play or die, you know? So I learned how to play it.
Let me see now. How many choruses of ensemble do you all usually play at the beginning of a tune?
Oh, you're gonna have to break that down for me now.
I mean, would you, uh, would you play, go through the melody once or twice?

Well, uh, usually once, huh? That's, uh, yeah, we'll go through it. Most of the time once. Most of the time once, then, uh, each, uh, instrument will take his solo. Then, uh, we'll take two choruses at the end, see, knock it out in two choruses.
Sometimes you play pairs, don't you?
Yeah, I will sometimes, uh, uh, maybe a...
Oh, the E-E-I-R-S.

A clarinet and the, uh, the trombone might, uh, take half, each one will take half a chorus. Maybe the piano and the banjo might take half and half. You know, something like that. Well, they might play it together. They might play it together. Well, uh, you have to...
I've got some pretty good, uh, two clarinet stuff up there.

Well, we use a double clarinet. We, uh, uh, well, uh, Bill, Bill Lee has been, uh, doubling with his, uh, soprano and his clarinet and his alto. And, uh, sometimes he and, uh, Briss will take a clarinet, uh, duet, you know. And it's, uh, I think, uh, Alphonse Pico and, uh, Big Eye, Louis Nelson, used to play that way. On a couple of recordings, they used a double clarinet. With Kid René.
Yeah. Kid René records.
Yeah. Got those.

Yeah, that's an old time thing. All the guys, tell me they used to do that. I've heard Emile Barnes and, uh, Albert Burbank together. They didn't have a trumpet play at one time, you know. And I sat in on the trombone. Yeah. And it was fun, you know, to hear them play like that. It sounded good. And John Handy and Willie Humphrey used to do that, too. Yeah.

Well, I don't think, uh, you'll see too many of the bands around the city now that do anything like that. No. I mean, it's just a novelty with us. Another thing, you hardly will see a banjo in your bands anymore. You see, or a toolbar, as far as that goes. You don't see things like that anymore. So I think that's what we are more or less capitalizing on, is the fact that we are reproducing the old, the real old sound, see. And, uh, that's what's keeping us going.
Do you ever work with, uh, any, uh, any less than the, uh, seven or six or seven instruments that you mentioned?

Sometimes, yeah. Well, uh, you take some of these, uh, patio parties we might play. They might want more of a, you know, a quiet and down music. So we, uh, we'll mute the trumpet, use a clarinet, piano, drums. Sometimes we'll operate with four pieces, sometimes five, sometimes six, sometimes a full eight. You know, it depends on the type of music that, uh, particular people will want at their party, you see. I mean, uh, I've seen times, uh, where we sound just a few pieces. We have, we sound as loud as the Eureka Brass Band. And I've also seen times where we sound like something that should have been in the blue room. We can hold it down there quiet at times, you see.
Do you ever play without bass or without piano or without drums or without this or without that?

Well, let's see. We've, uh, we've played without a piano already. We've played without drums already. We've played without bass already. Matter of fact, we even play without cornet already. You, you got a bunch of guys that just want to play and they know what they're doing. I mean, you could take a, a flute and a banjo and they could give a concert if both of them know what they're doing. You know, they could, they could, uh, be as effective as if they had a, maybe a six or seven piece band there.
Which instrument do you miss the most when you don't have it?

Uh, I would think maybe the... Stay out of the rhythm section. I would think the drum. I don't know. I mean, some, you know, maybe other people might have a different opinion of that, but I think the drum. A lot of times, I mean, uh, the drum, the, uh, bass will take the place of the drum. Or the banjo will take the place of the drum, you see. And I've just gotten so that, uh, I don't know if I could really play anymore without listening to a banjo sitting alongside of it. I've played already without a banjo and I just got into that, into that rut. I have to be listening to a banjo playing, see. The same thing with a trombone. I have to be listening to a trombone. Actually, by having those other instruments like that, they're helping me keep my timing, you know.
Yeah, well, that banjo sure gives you chords and everything. Helps you along. All that. I thought of another band that used to have two clarinets, Buddy Bolden. You've seen the picture of that?
Oh. With two clarinets? I'll show it to you.
Willie Warner. I'll show you that picture sometime. Yeah, that's an old tradition, you know. Get some good stuff that way. I'm just about to run out. How about you?

Oh, I tell you, when it gets, uh, when it gets on the subject of jazz, I could, I could talk on and on and on. But if I didn't have to run off and go put out flyers this afternoon, I would stay here all day.
I thought of one thing I could ask you. Who some of your favorite clarinet players were, for example.

What are you saying? Uh, I liked, uh, Alphonse Piku. I liked, uh, I liked what, I liked Albert Burbank. Uh, George Lewis. I think I like them all. I mean, if the guys can play, you can't help them like them. You gotta appreciate what they're doing, you know. I just like them all. Anybody that plays jazz, I like, you know, I will listen to.
What about trombone players?

Trombone? Uh, well, I'll have to say, uh, Archie Rogers, as far as I'm concerned, is one of the best in the city. I mean, maybe a lot of other people don't know that or have never heard him play. But personally, I think he's one of the best. Then, uh, Bob Havens is good. Bob Havens, uh, plays with Hurts Grove. He's good. Then, uh, I like Jim Robinson. I could go on, I could think of quite a few of them, but offhand, you know.
I just want you offhand. Yeah. I prefer to have that, you know, kind of.
Have you been to many, uh, parades that the Negro bands were playing? Uh, uh, on socials?

No, I can't say that I have. I think I maybe one of the few that live in New Orleans that hadn't been to a Negro funeral. You've never been there any. Uh, from what I can understand, uh, this boy, Joe Lyde, that used to play con-ed with the, uh, Last Straws, he'd march with the Negro, uh, parades already at funerals. He'd, uh, he'd march with them.
Mardi Gras, he was, uh. He played the Zulu. He played the Zulu parade almost all the way through then.
Yeah. She could get Miss Hon, Kid She could talk about that. And then he played Arthur Ogles funeral, too, you know.

Well, you know, all in all, uh, Joe Lyde, Joe Lyde was, wasn't only a musician. He was a pretty good entertainer while he was sitting on a bandstand. Uh, you know, and that's, that's why I always felt I had a big pair of shoes to fill when I went in this group. Cause, uh, as far as a showman, I mean, I'm nothing to look at, you know. But Joe, Joe would put on a flow show and play. Well, Joe went beyond and I paid him on something.
You know, he got too wild.

Well, you know, um, I, I, that's the first time I've seen that. Uh, one night, uh, they were playing a job someplace. Joe was, uh, playing connet and I just happened to be at this particular place. And Joe needed a mute for one of the tunes he was playing. So he had a half glass of beer sitting on a table. So he picks a glass up, throws the bell on the floor and uses the glass for a mute. And I mean, you know, you just don't see things like that every place, you know. But, uh, it was, it was real effective and I, I've used it several times myself. I used a plain drinking glass for a mute.
That just shows, uh, how Joe had, at one time, a one track mind. See, any other trumpet playing a little drop of beer.
That's right. I seen Joe show up for a job with a blue sock on an orange sock one time. No shoes. With the sandals.
Yeah.
Dressed to kill, but he had a pair of sandals on. Yeah. Joe just didn't care. All he cared for was to play his music, see.
Well, Kid Thomas is about the best one with the water glass around time. Does he use that?
Yeah, he's good with it.
And Panama is his specialty on that. Uh, let's see. Now, Joe, what else did he do? He owned Tiger Ride, you know, they had that whole lot of Tiger chorus. Did you ever see that?
Uh, where he would, uh, roar or yell.
Yeah, well, he, but he'd pull, when it came to hold that Tiger, he'd pull up a Christmas horn and blow it. That was really great.

I tell you, anybody, anybody that did see Joe in action, to me, Joe was the typical old, old, old time jazz musician. He just didn't care. He just wanted to play music. And, uh, I don't know, I've always admired Joe. I like Joe. I like his style. I like the way, maybe I, I would never think of action. I would never think of acting the way Joe acted on a bandstand, you understand? But, I mean, you had to appreciate what he was doing. Everything he did was just part of the show, you know?

I guess his, his personality is like Jeff Salsa told me one time. Jeff is a guy who goes to school, what's he studying? Philosophy? Psychology. Psychology. And, uh, he figured out one time, from talking to, talking and listening to George Gaynor and Jim Robinson, or maybe George talk about Jim, or something about those guys, that, that the old New Orleans style musician wasn't just a style of playing.
It was the character too, I believe. It was an absolute personality. Yeah.
With the, uh, with the guy. I mean, you just didn't play your art or anything. You, you, if you were a musician, well, that's what you were, and you weren't anything else.

Uh, incidentally, uh, Joe, Joe was a great, uh, Shakespearean fan, you know? Joe read Shakespeare every night of his life, man. And, I think when he graduated from high school, his mother had given him a, uh, oh, I think comedy tragedy and something or else, you know, all about Shakespeare. And, uh, it got to be like a tonic with him. Uh, you might say a, a sleep inducer. He had to read a few lines of Shakespeare every night before he went to sleep, you know? And, I mean, it was things like that that made a character of Joe, you know?

Well, Johnny Lane is the same. He sits up on the stand. This is a guy from Chicago that studied under Jimmy Newman. He sits up on the stand. On the stand. He might have had it right the first time. But anyways, he sits on the stand and reads Shakespeare, you know, between numbers. And Joe's Boonies will be playing with him. And he'll say, well, the next number is dedicated to our boss. High psychiatry. You know?

Well, I tell you, I've seen, uh, I've seen Archie Rogers in between numbers almost go to sleep on the bandstand. He'll, to me, he actually looks like he dozes. And on the next tune, he's as live as can be.
When you guys did that? They saved their lip, that wifey. Now having a long job. You fall asleep during the numbers.
Roll up that old King B, ready for the next tune.

I hear a trumpet player that I worked, right up around Tuscaloosa, Alabama, one night in Birmingham. He got pretty loaded and, uh, he went to sleep while we were playing, uh, uh, loud up-tempo number. So they let him sleep and they woke him up in the middle of the next number, which was, uh, one, if you pardon the expression, a belly-rubbing number. So he jumped up and he started playing this real hot, loud bass number right in the middle of the slow one. They told him to shut up and he sat back down and went to sleep and they woke him up again to take us over and, no, they woke him up again at intermission. He thought the job was over, so he packed up and left.

You know, well, speaking of Alabama, getting back to Alabama, uh, Briss brought my attention to it the other night. I really had forgotten about it. But, uh, we were playing when the Saints go marching in. When we were playing his debutant deal. And, uh, to me, I mean, the Saints is more of a, you know, it's just the same thing. You're playing the same thing over and over and over and over again, say, until the tune is finished. But, uh, that particular night, my finger got caught between two of the valves on my horn. And, uh, honestly, that's the best and the hardest I've ever played on the Saints. I don't know, I don't know, I could never do it again, see. But actually, that's what happened. My finger got between the first and second valve. And that's the best the Saints ever came off for me.
Jeff told me about the time he got his neck tied stuck between the...
Yeah, he got his tie caught in the strings of his banjo, you know. And, boy.
Now, one of the musicians wear bow ties.
Something happened to Ice, too, didn't it? One night?

Oh, uh, when we were, we were playing over in Europe, Ice broke a string on his bass. He plays his two-string bass. And he broke a string on his, on his bass. And the only thing that could be had was a regular bass, a real bass. They put it in his hands and he played it. He played just as good as he'd ever played. He played a regular... Of course, he only used the two strings, but I mean, he looked important standing up there with a real bass in his hands, you know.
Well, I know what he did, but I ain't gonna tell it.
I remember. Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. I remember.

How's it going? How much longer? I guess that's one of the hazards of the occupation, you know. Maybe we'd better... Maybe we'd better just run it off, you know, and get packed up and everything. Cause he's gonna be late.
